ego.name: Alexander Hamilton
ego.summary: Alexander Hamilton rose from an impoverished childhood in the British Caribbean to become a Continental Army officer, constitutional advocate, lawyer, leading Federalist, and the first United States secretary of the treasury. He shaped early American public finance and constitutional politics before Aaron Burr mortally wounded him in a duel in 1804.

connections.relationship_description: Hamilton's mother supported the family in Nevis and Saint Croix after James A. Hamilton left the household. Her death in 1768 left Hamilton and James Jr. orphaned.
connections.notes: She supported the family through property and a small store in Christiansted.

connections.relationship_description: Elizabeth Schuyler Hamilton was Hamilton's wife and the center of his household through war, public service, and scandal. After his death, she preserved his papers and worked to protect his reputation.
connections.notes: Elizabeth assisted with his political writing, sustained the household through his public career, and preserved his papers and reputation after his death.

connections.relationship_description: Philip Schuyler was Elizabeth Hamilton's father and a Continental Army general. Hamilton's marriage into the Schuyler family connected him to an influential New York military and political circle.
connections.notes: Burr's 1791 Senate victory over Schuyler sharpened the political hostility between Burr and Hamilton.

connections.relationship_description: Hamilton's eldest child, Philip, was born in 1782 and was killed in a duel with George Eacker in 1801. Hamilton and Elizabeth remained at their son's side as he died.
connections.notes: Philip's death deeply affected Hamilton and preceded Hamilton's own fatal duel by less than three years.

connections.relationship_description: Washington brought Hamilton onto his headquarters staff in 1777 and relied on him for military correspondence and planning. He later chose Hamilton as the first secretary of the Treasury.
connections.notes: Washington's trust gave Hamilton access to military and national political leadership despite his outsider background.

connections.relationship_description: Madison worked with Hamilton on constitutional reform and joined him and John Jay in writing The Federalist Papers. Their alliance broke down over Hamilton's financial program and the opposing parties that emerged in the 1790s.
connections.notes: Their constitutional collaboration gave way to major conflict over Hamilton's financial program and the emerging party system.

connections.relationship_description: Hamilton and Jay collaborated as authors of The Federalist Papers during the New York ratification campaign of 1787–1788. Jay also helped Hamilton gain a Revolutionary War artillery commission through his New York political connections.
connections.notes: Their alliance joined constitutional advocacy to the Federalist political network in New York.

connections.relationship_description: The Presbyterian minister tutored and mentored the young Hamilton in Saint Croix. In 1772, Knox submitted Hamilton's hurricane letter for publication in the Royal Danish-American Gazette, helping inspire local support for Hamilton's education in North America.
connections.notes: Knox's intervention helped turn Hamilton's writing ability into an opportunity to leave Saint Croix.

connections.relationship_description: Hamilton boarded with Mulligan after arriving in New York in 1772 and again while preparing for and entering King's College. Mulligan also assisted him in selling cargo intended to fund his education.
connections.notes: Mulligan provided practical support during Hamilton's crucial migration from Saint Croix to New York.

connections.relationship_description: Laurens and Hamilton became close friends as fellow officers on George Washington's staff during the Revolutionary War. They corresponded during periods of separation and shared strong commitments to the American cause.
connections.notes: Laurens's death in 1782 ended one of Hamilton's most emotionally important wartime friendships.

connections.relationship_description: Jefferson served with Hamilton in Washington's first cabinet and opposed Hamilton's financial program. Their conflict helped define the Federalist and Democratic-Republican parties.
connections.notes: Despite their philosophical conflict, Hamilton supported Jefferson over Burr in the contingent presidential election of 1800.

connections.relationship_description: Burr was Hamilton's New York legal and political adversary. Hamilton opposed Burr in the presidential contest of 1800 and the New York governor's race of 1804. Their conflict ended when Burr challenged Hamilton to a duel.
connections.notes: Their long-running political antagonism culminated in one of the most consequential duels in American history.

connections.relationship_description: Hamilton's father lived with Rachel Faucette and their sons in the Caribbean before abandoning the family during Hamilton's childhood. Hamilton later wrote him a detailed account of the 1772 Saint Croix hurricane.
connections.notes: His departure contributed to the family's poverty and insecurity.

connections.relationship_description: Hamilton's older brother shared his childhood in Nevis and Saint Croix and was orphaned with him after their mother's death in 1768. The brothers were later separated when James apprenticed to a carpenter.
connections.notes: Their early lives were shaped by the same precarious household circumstances.

connections.relationship_description: Catherine Van Rensselaer Schuyler was Elizabeth Hamilton's mother and part of the Albany household Hamilton joined through marriage. She belonged to the Schuyler family circle that became Hamilton's extended family in New York.
connections.notes: Her household formed part of Hamilton's extended family setting during and after the Revolution.

connections.relationship_description: After the Revolutionary War, Hamilton returned to New York City and began a legal practice in partnership with Richard Harison in 1783.
connections.notes: Their practice represented Hamilton's transition from military service into law and New York commercial life.

connections.relationship_description: Angelica Schuyler Church was Elizabeth Hamilton's older sister and a member of Hamilton's close family circle. She and Hamilton maintained a substantial surviving correspondence.
connections.notes: Their surviving letters have prompted speculation about romance, but the documented relationship clearly includes close family friendship and correspondence.

connections.relationship_description: Hamilton opposed President John Adams's reelection campaign in 1800, publicly attacking Adams's leadership and contributing to the division of the Federalist Party. Adams's approach to France and the Quasi-War was a central point of contention.
connections.notes: Their conflict damaged Federalist unity and helped clear the path for Jefferson's victory in 1800.

category_summaries.summary: Hamilton's family life began in a precarious Caribbean household. Rachel Faucette's death left him and James Jr. without parents. His 1780 marriage brought him into the Schuyler family of New York, and Elizabeth Hamilton managed their household through his public career and preserved his papers after his death.

Hamilton's professional circle carried him from Saint Croix to national office. Hugh Knox and Hercules Mulligan helped him reach New York, while Washington gave him responsibility at Continental Army headquarters and later the Treasury. Work with Madison and Jay during the ratification campaign joined his legal, military, and constitutional careers.

Hamilton's friendships helped him enter New York life and endure the Revolution. Mulligan gave practical support when Hamilton arrived from Saint Croix. John Laurens became a close wartime friend, and correspondence with the Schuyler circle kept family and political life closely connected.

Hamilton's political opponents shaped the conflicts of the new republic. Disputes with Jefferson and Madison over public finance helped form rival national parties. His break with John Adams divided the Federalists, and his opposition to Burr's 1804 candidacy led to the dispute that ended in their duel.
